grammar_topic: uses of the infinitive with to; uses of the gerund (verb + -ing)
title: Trying to Change
body: Every January, Rustam decides to change something about his life. This year, he's chosen to stop eating sugar and to start running every morning. He remembers avoiding exercise for years, always finding an excuse not to go. 'I enjoy sleeping more than jogging,' he used to joke with his colleagues. But after visiting the doctor, he agreed to try a healthier routine. Waking up early was the hardest part; he kept forgetting to set his alarm properly. Slowly, he managed to build a habit, and running became less painful. He also decided to stop drinking coffee after six in the evening, hoping to sleep better. His wife suggested cooking dinner together instead of ordering food, so they started preparing meals every night. By March, Rustam had learned to enjoy running, something he never expected to happen. 'I don't mind waking up early anymore,' he admits, tying his shoelaces before sunrise. Changing old habits, he realizes, takes more patience than he expected.

grammar_topic: have to, don't have to, must, mustn't
title: The Exam Room Rules
body: Before the exam starts, the supervisor reads out the rules to the nervous students. 'You must switch off your phones completely,' she says, 'and you mustn't bring any notes into the room.' Students don't have to bring their own pens, since the school provides them, but they have to bring a valid student card. 'You mustn't talk to anyone once the exam begins,' the supervisor warns, walking between the desks. Latecomers don't have to worry too much — they still have to finish at the same time as everyone else, with less time to write. Halfway through, a girl raises her hand; she has to ask for more paper. 'You don't have to raise your hand for that,' the supervisor smiles, 'just walk quietly to my desk.' Students who finish early mustn't leave immediately; they have to wait until the final bell rings. Outside, parents wait nervously, though they know they mustn't enter the building until the exam officially ends.

title: What Should I Do?
body: Farida can't decide whether to change her job, so she calls her older sister for advice. 'You should make a list of the good and bad things about your current job,' her sister suggests. 'You shouldn't decide something this important in one evening.' Farida admits she's been unhappy for months, but she's afraid of starting somewhere new. 'You should talk to your manager first,' her sister continues, 'maybe things can improve without you leaving.' Farida wonders if she should also ask for a higher salary while she's at it. 'You shouldn't be afraid to ask,' her sister laughs, 'the worst answer is just no.' They talk for almost an hour, discussing every possible option. In the end, Farida decides she should try talking to her manager before making any big decision. 'You should call me after the meeting,' her sister says. 'And you shouldn't worry so much beforehand — you always find a solution.'

grammar_topic: if + present, will + infinitive (first conditional); possessive pronouns
title: Whose Picnic Is It Anyway?
body: 'If it doesn't rain tomorrow, we'll have the picnic in the park,' Aziza tells her friends. 'If it rains, we'll move everything to my place instead.' Everyone agrees, though nobody wants to carry the heavy basket — it's not mine, someone insists, it's yours, another replies, pointing at a different friend. If the basket is actually his, he'll have to carry it himself. Aziza checks whose blanket they're bringing; hers is too small for six people, so they need a bigger one. 'If Dilshod brings his blanket, we won't need mine at all,' she decides. If everyone arrives on time, they'll catch the best spot near the lake. If someone forgets their food, they'll simply share everyone else's. By the time Saturday arrives, the weather looks perfect, and if nothing changes, the picnic will finally happen exactly as planned — with whichever blanket, and whichever basket, someone remembers to bring.

title: If I Won the Lottery
body: 'If I won the lottery, I would buy a small house by the sea,' Aziz tells his friends during their usual coffee break. 'I wouldn't quit my job completely, though — I'd probably work part-time.' His friend disagrees. 'If I had that much money, I'd stop working immediately and travel for a year.' Someone else jokes that if he became rich suddenly, his relatives would appear from nowhere, asking for loans. 'If I were you, I'd keep it a secret,' Aziz warns, only half joking. They imagine what they would do with the first million: some would help their parents, others would invest in a small business. 'If money weren't a problem, would you still do the same job?' Aziz asks the group. Most admit they wouldn't, though a few say they'd miss the daily routine. By the end of the break, nobody has won anything, but everyone returns to work slightly happier, having spent ten minutes living a different life.

grammar_topic: present perfect + for and since; present perfect or past simple? (2)
title: Friends Since School
body: Malika and Nodira have known each other since primary school, almost twenty years now. They've lived in different cities for the last five years, but they've stayed close friends since university. 'I haven't seen you properly since your wedding,' Malika says, hugging her old friend at the café. 'I know, I've been so busy since I started the new job,' Nodira replies. They last met in person two years ago, when Nodira visited briefly for a family event. Since then, they've only spoken on video calls, usually late at night. 'Do you remember when we got lost in the old town?' Malika laughs, recalling a trip they took years ago. Nodira has worked at the same company for three years now and finally feels settled. 'I moved to this city last spring,' Malika explains, 'so we're neighbours again, for the first time since school.' They order more tea, in no hurry to end a conversation they've been waiting years to have properly.

grammar_topic: expressing movement (prepositions and verbs); word order of phrasal verbs
title: Across the Finish Line
body: The runners climb over the wooden wall, crawl under the low net, and jump across the muddy pool without stopping. Jahongir runs through the forest path, then splashes straight into the cold river crossing. He climbs up the steep hill, breathing heavily, and slides down the other side on purpose, laughing. Near the end, he has to carry a heavy tyre from one point to another before he can put it down again. His friend, running just behind him, calls out to cheer him on. Jahongir picks up his pace and pushes himself forward across the final field. Volunteers hand out water bottles as runners rush past them towards the finish. He climbs one last rope wall, drops down onto soft sand, and finally crosses the line, exhausted but proud. His friend catches up with him a minute later, and they both sit down to rest. 'I nearly gave up back there,' Jahongir admits, 'but I kept going anyway.'

title: How Our Bread Is Made
body: Every morning at four o'clock, the bakery on our street is opened by the same two bakers, before anyone else is awake. First, the flour is mixed with water, salt, and yeast in a large metal bowl. The dough is then kneaded by hand for almost twenty minutes until it becomes smooth. Afterwards, it's left to rise for an hour, covered by a thin cloth. Once it has risen, the dough is shaped into round loaves by the older baker, who has done this job for thirty years. Each loaf is then placed carefully into the hot oven, where it's baked for exactly forty minutes. While the bread is being baked, the smell fills the whole street, and customers are already queuing outside. By seven o'clock, the first loaves are taken out and are sold within minutes. 'This bread isn't made with any machines,' the baker tells a curious customer. 'Everything here is still done the old way.'

title: Ask the Teacher
body: Mr. Aliyev used to teach maths at our school for almost thirty years, and he still visits every autumn. 'This building used to look completely different,' he tells the current students, pointing at the modern hallway. 'We used to have wooden desks, and there used to be a big tree right where the canteen is now.' Some students find it hard to imagine a school without computers. 'I used to walk two hours to get here every morning,' he continues, smiling at their surprised faces. He used to give extra maths classes on Saturdays, something the school doesn't offer anymore. 'Did you use to enjoy teaching us?' a student asks curiously. 'I used to worry I wasn't strict enough,' he laughs, 'but looking back, I think I was exactly strict enough.' Before he leaves, he reminds them that homework used to be much harder in his day, though nobody quite believes him.

title: Neither Do I
body: 'I might go hiking this weekend, if the weather stays good,' Sabina tells her colleague during lunch. 'So might I,' he replies, surprised. 'I don't really enjoy crowded places on weekends,' Sabina admits. 'Neither do I,' he says, laughing at how similar their plans sound. 'I might invite a few friends, but I haven't decided yet.' 'Neither have I,' he replies, 'I might just go alone if nobody's free.' They discover they might both be going to the same mountain trail, at roughly the same time. 'I've never actually hiked that trail before,' Sabina says. 'Neither have I, but I might try the shorter path first.' 'So might I — the longer one might be too difficult for one afternoon.' By the end of lunch, they've quietly arranged to meet at the trail entrance on Saturday morning. 'I might bring a picnic,' Sabina adds. 'So will I,' he laughs. 'Looks like neither of us needs to hike alone this weekend.'

title: The Meeting That Already Ended
body: By the time Karim arrived at the office, the meeting had already started without him. He had left home early, but a sudden traffic jam had delayed him for almost an hour. When he finally reached the meeting room, everyone had already left; the discussion had finished ten minutes earlier. His manager had sent an email that morning, moving the meeting time, but Karim hadn't checked his phone since breakfast. He realized he had missed an important decision about his own project. His colleague explained that the team had already agreed on a new deadline, one Karim hadn't known about. He felt annoyed that nobody had called him directly. Later, he discovered that his manager had actually tried to call twice, but Karim's phone had been on silent all morning. By lunchtime, Karim had accepted that the mistake was partly his own, and he promised himself he would never leave his phone on silent again.

title: Who Said What?
body: At the family dinner, everyone starts arguing about who said what earlier that day. 'You said you'd finish the shopping,' Malika tells her husband. He replies that he told her he would try, not that he would definitely finish it. Their daughter mentions that grandma had said the soup needed more salt, though grandma insists she said no such thing. 'Who broke the vase in the hallway?' Malika asks, looking around the table. Nobody answers directly; her son says his sister told him it was already broken before he touched it. 'What happened at school today?' Malika asks, trying to change the subject. Her daughter explains that the teacher had asked who wanted to join the choir, and almost everyone raised their hand. 'Who wants dessert?' Malika finally asks, and this time every hand goes up immediately, without a single argument. Later, washing the dishes, Malika smiles, thinking that in this house, someone always says something different from what actually happened.
